💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

It has been revealed that the best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

Recent findings suggest that the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

Industry observers note that there were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” remarked Kerry Stauffer.

It has been revealed that last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Recent findings suggest that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Recent findings suggest that rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Sources indicate that along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he states the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

It has been revealed that tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka intends to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

💪 Into the High Sierra: ❄️ Snow, Ice & Forrester Pass 🏔️

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I packed up from my stealth spot before daybreak and used the park bathroom to change and brush my teeth.
  • It has been revealed that sitting at a picnic table in the shade, I pulled up my blog.
  • I picked at my leftover Chinese food for breakfast as I sorted through my resupply and packed my backpack for the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I packed up from my stealth spot before daybreak and used the park bathroom to change and brush my teeth.

It has been revealed that sitting at a picnic table in the shade, I pulled up my blog. That’s when I realized I had forgotten to hit publish on the post I had scheduled for the previous week. I rushed to get it published, feeling frustrated with myself and the growing pressure to keep up with my writing. Once my blog was published online, I spent the remainder of the morning working on my next entry.

I picked at my leftover Chinese food for breakfast as I sorted through my resupply and packed my backpack for the trail.

Sources indicate that walking through town, I stopped at Carl’s Jr. for a Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese and a strawberry milkshake. I packed the burger away to eat later on the trail.

Before hitching out, I stopped at Elevation Gear, where I finished my ice cream and spent a few minutes visiting with Marble, Electrolyte, and Pickles while telling them my plans.

Walking along the road toward the Horseshoe Meadow turnoff, I dropped my pack to hitch. I stood with my thumb out, hoping for a ride. A few vehicles stopped to offer rides, but they were heading either to Whitney Portal or the Alabama Hills. A couple of other drivers pulled over only to tell me they didn’t have room.

In a recent development, the gestures were kind, but each time a vehicle stopped, my hopes went up. Having them dashed by another apology made the wait even more discouraging.

After 30 minutes with no luck, I grabbed my backpack and walked farther out of town.

A farmer working in a field across the street told me he had been watching me try to hitch a ride down the road. He wished me luck.

“The right ride will come.” I told him.

Five minutes later, a car pulled over.

Recent findings suggest that the driver, Taquito, told me he was a Triple Crown thru-hiker from Omaha. He was on vacation, hiking and providing trail magic to hikers. We talked about hiking, his Triple Crown experiences, and the trail magic he was sharing with hikers. He took me all the way to the Horseshoe Meadow trailhead.

At the trailhead, Taquito offered me even more trail magic in the form of Gatorade, an apple, and Gummy Clusters. Taking advantage of the nearby trash cans, I drank the Gatorade, ate the apple, and demolished my double burger before heading out on the trail. I tucked the Gummy Clusters away for later.

Leaving the trailhead at 4:30 p.m., I began my hike into the mountains. Lone Pine had been hot during the day, now, in elevation the evening air was getting cold. The loose, sandy trail made walking difficult, especially with my heavy backpack. I moved slowly, tired and a little stressed about finding a place to camp before the elevation started.

Sources indicate that I spent too much time looking off-trail for flat spots. Two miles in, the trees began to grow thicker, I suddenly came across a sandy clearing with a rabbit. Seeing it hopping around so carefree made the area feel safe and inviting. I liked the idea of sharing this little clearing with the rabbit, so I decided this was where I would camp.

I used my newly acquired ice axe to scrape and level the sandy ground, making a flat spot for my tent.

According to recent reports, for dinner, I made a Frito taco bowl with dehydrated pea-protein “beef” and dried refried beans. It hit the spot after a long day. With a full belly, a newly leveled tent spot, and a rabbit for manufacturer, I crawled into my tent. Too tired to write, I fell asleep around 8 p.m. with a bit of daylight still lingering. I had a long way to go, but at least I was back in the mountains.

Sources indicate that I woke up at 3 a.m. to a dark, chilly morning. I was camped on the Cottonwood Pass Trail, 2.6 miles from its junction with the PCT at Mile 751.4. Nearly 1,200 feet lower in elevation. I opened one of my tent vestibules to help ventilate the condensation before burrowing back into my quilt for a little more rest.

Recent findings suggest that at 4:15 a.m., I woke to the howling of coyotes. It made me smile. I love being in nature. Still tucked into my quilt, I reached for my headlamp in the top pocket of my backpack, where I always keep it. Although I normally sleep with it around my neck, I knew exactly where to find it.

Recent findings suggest that while getting breakfast ready, I also pulled out my snacks for the day. I try to eat my heavier, bulkier foods first to lighten my pack. As I was packing up, I spotted Spicy Bite (Southern California) hiking toward town. He graciously offered to carry out my trash. Everything was inside a Ziploc bag, including half a family-size bag of Fritos that I had hiked in. I slipped the bag into his backpack without making him take it off. One less thing to carry!

In a recent development, A little after 7 a.m., I was hiking across a green, grassy meadow covered in frost. The sun hadn’t yet risen over the mountains, and the air grew colder as I approached a stream. After crossing it, I looked up at the steep mountainside ahead. I checked my map, trying to figure out where the trail passed through the snow-covered pass above. I began preparing myself for the climb.

The trail entered a pine forest and began to switchback.

Industry observers note that the sun began to warm the earth. Chipmunks scurried over the white boulders and fallen logs along the trail. At the last switchback before the top, I stopped for a break. I was above 11,000 feet and beginning to notice a slight headache coming on. After five minutes, I pushed on to the top and finally rejoined the PCT.

Recent findings suggest that just minutes later, I stopped at the first trickle of flowing water. My headache was slowly developing, and my stomach wasn’t feeling right. I needed to hydrate and give myself time to adjust before continuing farther into the Sierras. I spent the next hour and a half sitting beside the trail at 11,132 feet, drinking water and trying to stay warm. My headache improved slightly, but I still wasn’t feeling quite right.

In a recent development, pushing to higher elevations can be dangerous. In 2022, I had been just a few days behind a young hiker who lost her life on Forester Pass due to altitude-related problems. That experience had stayed with me and reminded me not to take the mountains lightly.

As I packed up, I noticed another hiker continuing past the Lone Pine exit. It was Diva (Tennessee), who had already built up his trail legs after hiking the Appalachian Trail and then the Florida Trail over the past year. He was planning to continue north to Kearsarge Pass.

In a recent development, we hiked together to the frozen Chicken Spring Lake, where we met a group of local high school students and their teachers. The students were about to graduate and were on a 20-day backpacking trip.

It has been revealed that having manufacturer lifted my spirits, even though I still wasn’t feeling 100%. Before leaving the lake, I noticed my feet were feeling swollen and my shoes were getting tight. With the altitude already on my mind, it was another thing I was paying attention to. I took an ibuprofen, collected a little more water, and said goodbye as Diva continued north.

Sources indicate that as I climbed over the next pass and entered Kings Canyon National Park, the landscape opened up to beautiful views. A meadow stretched out to my left, while the trail wrapped around the mountainside. To my right, the majestic pink and white rock walls of Cirque Peak towered above me at 12,900 feet.

I stopped for lunch and noticed dark clouds gathering in the distance. I moved more snacks into my hip-belt pocket. With most of my elevation gain behind me for the day, I wasn’t too concerned about being caught in a storm while exposed on a climb, though I did pick up my pace.

As thunder rumbled in the dark clouds, I hurried to the next water source. I found a few flat spots nearby and collected water, letting my gravity filter do its work while I set up my tent. With the storm moving in, I wanted to get settled before it arrived.

Sources indicate that happy with my setup, I was about to put my gear inside when I looked up. Above my tent, I saw one dead tree leaning against another, with yet another dead tree on the opposite side. With thunder sounding closer, I promptly decided to move my tent. I relocated to a completely different spot a short distance away.

Another hiker, Scott (Upcoming Zealand), came down the trail. He was planning to continue a few more miles before setting up for the night. I finally threw my gear into my tent just as it started to hail.

Small hailstones continued falling steadily. I occasionally bumped the sides of my tent to knock off the accumulating ice. It was only 5 p.m., but I was happy to be inside and dry, with enough water for the night.

I boiled water and mixed half a Mountain House pepperoni pizza meal with half a chicken alfredo meal.

Industry observers note that after the hail stopped, the golden sun came streaming through the pine trees. Tiny white pieces of hail were scattered across the ground, contrasting with the beautiful green landscape.

I brushed my teeth and placed my bear can behind a large fallen tree as the sun dipped below the mountains.

Crawling into my tent, I thought about how far I had come. I was proud of myself for making it this far on the trail and stepping into the high-altitude Sierras. It had taken bravery and strength to venture this far into the wilderness on my own. Even with the cold, I was genuinely happy to be surrounded by such a beautiful place. I felt grateful to be there, with a deep respect for the mountains and the wilderness I am fortunate enough to experience.

It has been revealed that at 3:45 a.m., my alarm pulled me out of sleep. I wanted to eat up any food that required cooking today so that tomorrow, when I pushed over Forrester Pass, I could just grab bars and snacks and keep moving.

After boiling water, I made oatmeal and a mix of hot cocoa and coffee.

It has been revealed that part of the reason I struggle to hike with others is that I’m a slower hiker and take longer to get out of camp. I get frustrated when I’m the last one to leave, and that frustration can often affect my attitude throughout the day.

This morning, I realized that taking my time getting out of camp was a form of self-care. When I give myself time to get everything done without rushing, I’m happier and more relaxed. I also know I’ve taken care of everything at camp and haven’t forgotten any chores.

At 7 a.m., I continued my hike. The trail descended toward Rock Creek, where it opened into a beautiful grassy valley surrounded by snow-covered mountains. Water was flowing everywhere. It was a completely different landscape from the desert I’d been hiking through the past two months.

As I approached Rock Creek, I passed established campsites, a few with hikers still packing up. The creek was rushing, and the morning air was cold.

The stepping stones used later in the year were covered in inches of rushing water. Looking downstream, I spotted an old fallen tree with no bark. It would likely be slippery with the frost that morning. A little farther down, I saw a newer-looking fallen tree across the creek. Thinking this might be an option, I started climbing onto it, but some of the bark slipped off, revealing a smooth, slippery surface. Looking farther along the log, I noticed more sections where the bark was missing.

According to recent reports, I hiked back upstream, past the trail, but didn’t find any better options for a dry crossing. I felt most comfortable getting my shoes wet, hoping that if I crossed on the rocks, I could at least keep the rest of my clothing dry.

I tried stepping across the rocks first. As soon as both feet were on the slippery rocks, I decided it would be better to just cross the creek. Plunging my legs into the freezing current, the water reached my knees. Even part of my rolled-up pants got wet as I climbed out on the other side.

I met a NOBO JMT hiker named Will (California), who had taken off his shoes to cross the creek and was putting them back on.

At the top of the next hill, I took a break on a boulder with a view, dreaming of French toast with syrup, maybe even peanut butter.

Scott from the day before walked up while I was taking a break. This was when we officially met.

Hiking through a rocky boulder field, I heard black-capped Chickadees chirping something that sounded like the word “cheeseburger.” Every time I heard it, I couldn’t help but laugh and found myself getting hungry!

Recent findings suggest that reaching Crabtree Meadow, I crossed Whitney Creek using a log. I felt a little uneasy about my balance with my backpack and how high the log was above the creek, but I made it across. I was proud of myself!

After crossing Whitney Creek, I passed the first trail junction leading to Mount Whitney.

The PCT climbed through exposed switchbacks with some great views. I stopped halfway up to apply sunscreen.

Passing the second junction to Whitney, I was slightly tempted to take it, but continued hiking the PCT. I didn’t have enough food to add the extra day and a half, and the last forecast I’d read was predicting snow in a few days.

I picked my way through some patchy snow before arriving at Wallace Creek. After hiking up and down the creek looking for a dry crossing, I couldn’t find one. This time I took off my shoes, socks, calf compression sleeves, and gaiters before crossing.

The creek was cold, the rocks were slippery, and the water was high enough to get the bottom of my shorts a little wet.

I dried my feet with a bandanna and let them air out for a bit before putting everything back on.

Industry observers note that clouds started rolling in as the afternoon continued. I needed to push to get as close to Forrester Pass as I could.

As I approached the climb up Substantial Horn Plateau, the clouds grew closer, and I could hear thunder rumbling. Seeing a cluster of trees about 300 feet off the trail, I crossed a small creek to take a break, eat a snack, and assess the storm.

With a snack in my stomach, most of the dark clouds had moved off to the south, though I could still hear thunder rumbling in the distance. I ventured back to the trail, still cautious as I headed toward a treeless area at 11,056 feet, with a metal bear canister in my backpack.

As I climbed onto Massive Horn Plateau, it began to snow. The clouds obscured some of the panoramic views of the Sierra mountains, though I could still see much of the surrounding landscape. I was exhausted and cold, and I wasn’t particularly happy about being out there in the weather. But stopping wasn’t even a consideration.

My last obstacle for the day was Tyndall Creek. One of the trail notes mentioned a more manageable crossing about a half-mile upstream. As I started heading upstream, a hiker on the other side spotted me and came down to the creek.

According to recent reports, I didn’t see him right away and couldn’t hear him over the rushing water. He pointed toward the spot where the trail crossed and told me to just cross there.

Again, I took off my shoes, socks, gaiters, and calf compression sleeves before stepping into the frigid water.

There were a few small groups of hikers scattered among the campsites. I found a semi-flat, semi-secluded spot and set up camp. I made dinner and got ready for bed. Tomorrow was going to be an early start. I was a little nervous about Forrester Pass. I had 5 miles to the top and didn’t want to be plunge-stepping down the north side in the afternoon. I was glad I wouldn’t have to cross Tyndall Creek in the morning.

According to recent reports, at 3:00 a.m., I woke to bright stars in the cold morning sky. I mixed coffee into cold water and packed snacks into my pockets. After packing up camp, I took off my puffy and hit the trail at 4:40 a.m.

Hiking in the early morning light, I didn’t need my headlamp. The colors in the sky were stunning.

The trail crossed small snowmelt creeks, weaving in and out of stream crossings. At one point, the melting snow had created a stream right across the trail.

My feet crunched over the frozen ground, and I slipped a bit on a patch of ice. I realized I needed to be more careful crossing snow bridges, especially with rushing water underneath.

In a recent development, the only person I saw that morning was Scott, who passed me. I was still hoping to find a hiking buddy for the pass, and I was glad everything was so frozen.

As I continued climbing, I kick-stepped up increasingly steep icy fields, trying to avoid the boulders that were beginning to melt and weaken the snow in the morning sun.

Industry observers note that as I looked up in awe at 13,897-foot Junction Peak next to it, Forrester Pass, at 13,120 feet, loomed ahead like a boss. I could see two people crossing over its scary icy chute above.

Just then, I heard someone hiking on the ice behind me. I was surprised to see Scott again. He had taken a break off trail, and I must have passed him at some point.

I told Scott we should hike together up and over the pass, and he agreed. I’m sure he did it just so I would feel more comfortable hiking it. Once we were out of the valley bowl, the switchbacks were mostly clear. They received afternoon sun each day.

Industry observers note that as I made my way toward Forrester Pass, I felt a mix of intimidation and excitement. The climb ahead was daunting, and the icy terrain made me nervous, especially the chute. I was more worried about crossing the chute than the north side, although it would turn out that I probably should have been more concerned about the other side. Still, I felt confident in my ability to tackle the challenge. Reaching Forrester Pass would be a huge milestone, both physically and personally. It was the highest point on the PCT, and I was excited to see what it would take to get there.

When we finally reached the ice chute, I watched Scott scoot across the iced-over, foot-shaped holes in the ice. I questioned whether I should take the time to put on my microspikes. I hadn’t worn them yet on the trail.

My heart started to race. I secured my microspikes to the bottom of each shoe and exchanged one of my trekking poles for my ice axe. I crossed the ice chute one foot at a time, never looking down and maintaining three points of contact. Just like that, I was on the rocky trail on the other side.

Thrilled to be over the ice chute, I hollered down into the valley below. Just a few more switchbacks to the highest point on the PCT!

As I attempted to take a drink of my coffee, I discovered that the liquid around the lid had frozen, and there were chunks of ice inside the bottle. Thirsty as I was, I laughed. How often do you get a frozen coffee with a view like this?

Recent findings suggest that as I crested the pinnacle of the PCT, Forrester Pass, I hollered at the top of my lungs in excitement. We stopped to take in the view and take photos on the blisteringly cold pass. Afterward, we decided it was too icy to glissade, so we would hike down instead. There was more snow on the north side because it received less sunlight during the early spring months. I was glad I had my microspikes. Scott didn’t have any.

Sources indicate that unable to see the trail, we followed footprints as we switchbacked down the ridge, eventually ending up farther out than we should have. Unaware that we were that far off trail, I told Scott I would probably be fine from there, and he picked up his pace.

Following the footprints, we ended up at the edge of the ridge. Scott climbed down over the snow and rocks and continued on. Dark, foggy clouds began rolling in. I hesitated, wondering whether I should backtrack alone to look for the trail or attempt to follow him. I was still reluctant to use my ice axe.

Sources indicate that just then, Scott slipped and slid, landing in a pile of rocks. He yelled out that he was hurt.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, Yak and Gezelle were already below us and rushed over to help. I tossed them my first-aid kit.

I decided it was unsafe to try to climb down with my heavy, off-balance backpack, so I took it off and lowered it down using my bear line.

In a recent development, by the time I safely reached the bottom, Scott had already continued hiking on his own. The girls were packing up the first-aid kit and shouldering their packs as two young hikers who had just glissaded down the pass hiked toward us.

In a recent development, they had been hiking with the girls and were fast hikers. We were really concerned about Scott, even though he had an SOS button. The guys hiked ahead to try to catch up with him.

The three of us women continued hiking downhill, passing stunning teal-blue alpine lakes and crossing streams alongside the roaring Bubbs Creek. We were surrounded by some of the most epic views of beautiful white granite peaks.

It has been revealed that at Mile 784, at an elevation of 10,961 feet, I took off my microspikes. Eventually, most of the snow was gone, replaced by puddles along the rocky trail and the occasional large snowdrift that I had to plunge-step through.

It has been revealed that below 10,000 feet and back in the trees, the girls stopped for a break while I continued hiking. When I reached Bubbs Creek, I noticed a downed tree upstream. I decided to take my shoes off and wade across instead. Waterfalls cascaded everywhere, and the creek was rushing with so much water. Along the trail, I also spotted a young buck.

two guys from earlier, who were taking a break on the side of the trail. They told me Scott was still alive and hadn’t bled out. This was where they had caught up to him, and he was still hiking at a good clip. I was happy to hear the news and relieved that he was doing okay.

With my early start, my quilt had some condensation on it when I packed up. I considered stopping to dry it out, but noticed a cooler breeze and clouds starting to roll in from the west. I wondered if we might get some precipitation.

I continued down the switchbacks toward Vidette Meadow. I was exhausted by the time I reached the trail junction, where there was a bear box. I found a spot a little farther off the trail and set up my tent around 12:30 p.m.

Sources indicate that I collected water and filtered 1.75 liters. After making my Chicken and Vegetable Rice Mountain House meal and having cocoa coffee, I settled in for a nap from 1:00–2:30 p.m. While I napped, my body heat helped dry the condensation from my quilt.

According to recent reports, after waking, I decided to stay at the lower elevation rather than climb higher because the weather was uncertain. I spent the afternoon blogging and relaxing at camp. I was almost out of food, and after eating a significant lunch, I settled for some candy and made tea. Around 7 p.m., I fell asleep again.

At 11:30 p.m., I woke to the sound of precipitation hitting my tent. It was barely sleeting. I checked the tension on my tent, then curled back into my quilt.

Recent findings suggest that in the morning, my tent was covered in a very thin layer of sleet that had slightly melted on contact and stuck to the tent. One guyline had slipped out of place, and a corner of the tent was sagging under the weight. The ground was dusted with tiny sleet pellets and snow.

Before putting on my shoes, I slipped a twist-tie snack bag over each foot. If my feet got wet in these temperatures, I might have trouble keeping them warm. I wanted to do everything I could to keep them dry.

Around 7:00 a.m., I left camp, making fresh tracks on the trail.

According to recent reports, not long after starting, I arrived at a wide stream feeding into the roaring Bubbs Creek. I picked my way across its multiple channels, stepping on fallen logs and large rocks while using my trekking poles for balance.

According to recent reports, I arrived at a trail junction, turned right, and began climbing out of the canyon. As I gained elevation, the trees began to thin, and the terrain gave way to solid rock. As I switchbacked across the cliffs, I had a beautiful view of Kings Canyon and could see the valley I had hiked down the day before. Forrester Pass itself was hidden behind a mountain.

Recent findings suggest that the Kearsarge Pinnacles, along with East and West Vidette Mountains, towered over the valley, dusted with snow. The scenery was so beautiful that it hardly looked real, with every detail highlighted by the white snow.

It has been revealed that crossing flowing streams and seasonal snowmelt, I was glad I had put the bags over my feet that morning. My shoes got damp, but my feet stayed dry and warm.

In a recent development, there was a brief relief from the climbing as I passed the first trail junction toward Bullfrog Lake and Kearsarge Pass. The plateau was flat and sandy, with a few scattered pine trees. I could see unfamiliar mountains towering in the distance and hear what sounded like military jets booming overhead, though I couldn’t see a single one.

I took the second trail junction, adding 7.6 bonus miles up and over Kearsarge Pass to the trailhead. As I climbed, the trees became increasingly sparse. Near the cutoff leading back down to Bullfrog Lake, I noticed a ranger’s note posted on a rock. It was titled “Bear Info” and warned hikers that bears in the area had gotten food from people and would continue trying to get more. It reminded hikers never to leave food unattended and to keep all food and scented items secured.

The note also included some rather unusual advice about what to do if you encountered a bear!

At 10:00 a.m., I reached Kearsarge Pass at 11,760 feet after hiking five miles and gaining 2,200 feet in elevation.

Inside the Sierras, the skies were partly cloudy with patches of blue. On the Highway 395 side, the sky was cloudy and gray, and I could see a storm blowing in from the north. I was relieved that I had beaten the storm to the pass.

Industry observers note that I met a hiker named Crush who was hiking back over the pass. Just then, it started to lightly snow, and it continued throughout the rest of my hike. I was cold as I began the long switchbacks down toward Onion Valley. Massive Pothole Lake was covered in ice, its surface a deep blue. On the other side of the lake, three people were practicing self-arresting with their ice axes on the snow.

Sources indicate that passing Gilbert Lake, I noticed patches of green grass and scattered trees around the partially frozen lake. The three men I’d seen practicing with their ice axes passed me on the trail. I was too shy to ask for a ride, thinking they would be long gone by the time I reached the trailhead.

It has been revealed that as the trail continued downhill, I had views of waterfalls cascading down the steep valley walls. In the final mile, the parking lot came into view. I could still see the three men, so I picked up my pace, hoping they were still at the trailhead. If they were, I was going to ask for a ride.

In a recent development, when I reached the parking lot, I hurried over to where the three men were sitting in their vehicles with the windows down. Thankfully, they had been waiting for me!

Frank and his sons had permits for Mount Whitney on Friday, weather permitting, and had been practicing with their ice axes at elevation. They were heading to Lone Pine in their two vehicles and offered me a ride.

I stopped at the post office in Lone Pine to pick up my new base layer. Frank and his sons then dropped me a few blocks away at the gear store, where I repacked my backpack.

In a recent development, I was hoping to get a bunk at The Hostel California in Bishop. The hostel was first come, first served, and with cellphone service concerns in the area since the windstorm back at Kennedy Meadows South, I wasn’t able to secure a spot ahead of time.

I hiked to the north edge of town and stuck out my thumb, hoping to catch a ride toward Bishop.

Someone pulled over, but they were only going as far as Independence. I thanked them but decided to hold out for a ride all the way to Bishop.

According to recent reports, mark, from Tehachapi, picked me up. He was heading past Bishop to retrieve his family’s RV at June Lake. His family had been camping there with their trailer when they decided to drive into Yosemite the previous day. It ended up snowing, and Tioga Road closed, leaving them unable to get back to their trailer. They had to drive home to Tehachapi, and Mark was now making the trip back to retrieve the RV.As we approached Bishop, I called The Hostel California to check for a bunk. Unfortunately, they were full. Not sure where to go that wouldn’t cost me over three bills, I asked Mark to drop me off at Smart & Final.

I picked up a bagged salad, a pint of ice cream, a gallon of milk, and a box of cereal for dinner and breakfast. Then I started walking down the snowy streets of Bishop.

Hotel prices were high because the Mule Days festival had just taken place. Heartbroken that the hostel was full and unsure whether I knew any other hikers in town, I started walking down the snowy main street, going from motel to motel asking for a hiker discount.

It has been revealed that by my third stop, I was struggling to hold back tears. If only I knew someone in town I could split a room with. The snowy weather had left the streets nearly empty.

Sources indicate that after leaving my fourth motel, I was considering stealth camping when an angel named Erine pulled over. She had seen me at the store earlier and noticed me wandering down the street. She was a local teacher.

She asked where I was headed. Not really sure myself, I explained that I was looking for a motel that might offer a discount for hikers.

When we arrived at the motel, Erine, the angel of a woman, paid for my room. She also made sure I got my backpack and groceries inside quickly because of the precipitation.

Recent findings suggest that before leaving, she gave me her phone number in case I needed anything while I was in Bishop and gave me a hug. Then she was gone.

After taking a shower and doing some laundry, I spiderwebbed my bear line around the room. There weren’t many good places to tie it off, but I managed to create a makeshift clothesline.

I spent some time blogging before eating half the salad for dinner. I also brushed the caps of my two Smartwater bottles, which I had been carrying since Mexico. It’s a chore I try to do in every town.

I fell asleep in a soft, warm bed with the TV on.

It has been revealed that the skies had cleared up in town. You could still see fresh snow covering the mountains, with clouds beginning to move back over them. I spent my morning eating cereal, drinking coffee, and blogging. It felt good to have time to catch up without feeling so rushed and to have a little less stress on my shoulders.

I received a group message and found out that Google was in town staying at the Motel 6. He offered to split his bed with me for the night.

When checkout time came, I walked down the road with my backpack to the Motel 6. Google and two other hikers had been there for days, and their gear was scattered around the room. I threw my backpack in a corner away from everyone else’s gear.

It has been revealed that there was a group wanting to go to Keough’s Hot Springs outside of town. I was unsure if I wanted to go, still having chores to do before leaving town. With snow still predicted in the mountains that day, I had no excuse not to go.

With no rideshares available, we started walking down the road and eventually found a hitch who even offered to take us the few miles off the main road to the hot springs.

Sources indicate that once there, we entered the bathhouse. There was a large, warm pool for swimming and a smaller, hot, shallow pool for soaking. The warm pool had no roof, offering a glimpse of the surrounding scenery. Dark storm clouds hung over the Sierra peaks, making being in the warm water feel even better.

After spending a few hours at the pool, most of it soaking in the hot water and enjoying a pretzel Google shared with me, the group walked the mile back to Highway 395 to hitch a ride to Bishop.

The storm had given the desert valley a beautiful, moody feel, with clouds draped over the White Mountains in front of us.

After returning to the motel with my resupply box, I set it aside to deal with tomorrow. I still hadn’t decided how many days of food I would need for the next stretch. With several challenging mountain passes ahead, I wanted to take some time to make sure I was prepared for what was coming. I spent the rest of the evening relaxing in the room while the others headed out for pub trivia and bowling. It was nice to have a quiet evening before heading back into the mountains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

In a recent development, the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

It has been revealed that otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

Sources indicate that at the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

In a recent development, “We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

  • This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In a recent development, in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

It has been revealed that “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

Recent findings suggest that inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” mentioned local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

In a recent development, many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#149347. Surviving The Worst-Case Scenario: Higher Inflation, Lower Asset Values

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2345 w)

Surviving The Worst-Case Scenario: Higher Inflation, Lower Asset Values

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation.
  • Sources indicate that post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way.
  • It has been revealed that if you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation. Yes, food costs more. Yes, tuition and health insurance went up again. But our stocks, our homes, and our private investments rose even faster. We felt richer, so we shrugged.

Sources indicate that post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way. Real estate is usually the last domino to fall. We are living in the worst-case scenario for anyone building or preserving wealth: higher prices and lower asset values at the same time.

It has been revealed that if you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone. My public equity portfolio is overweight tech, and it's taking a beating. I'm down around 20% from the highs, or more than three years of living expenses, and it hurts.

The only silver lining is that FIRE and debt don't mix, which has prevented me from going on margin and losing even more.

It has been revealed that say a household has $1 million in investments and spends $120,000 a year. With 3.7% inflation, its cost of living rises by about $4,400 a year.

Industry observers note that when that portfolio was up 20%, the household gained $200,000. That's 45 years' worth of extra inflation costs. Nobody complains about $4,400 when they're up $200,000.

In a recent development, now the portfolio is down 12%. That's a $120,000 loss, and the extra $4,400 a year in living costs hasn't gone anywhere. The household didn't just lose its cushion. It's paying more to live while owning less.

That's why the mood flipped so fast. The wealth effect works in reverse, and it works faster on the way down. Let's look at how we got here, where stocks could go, and how to survive until the bargain gets restored.

After Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the midterms, investors began pricing in a slower AI data-center buildout. The market began to correct.

Then Nvidia, due to the Jensen Huang debacle, and the rest of the AI complex kept sliding. The QQQ just finished its 9th-worst week since its 1999 launch, down 10.5%. That's the worst week since March 2020.

The S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on Nov 20, about 11.6% below its Oct 6 closing high of 7,819. Another ~9.5% decline to roughly 6,255 and we're officially in a bear market.

Whether you cheered or groaned on election night is irrelevant to your portfolio. The market reprices to future expectations.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, inflation refuses to cooperate. The last annual CPI reading was 3.7% in September. October prices rose 0.4% month-over-month, hotter than expected. Gasoline is up about 37% from a year ago. And the market is pricing in a Fed rate hike in December.

A Fed hiking into a falling stock market is not what the doctor ordered. But it is what we've got.

It has been revealed that here's what makes this downturn different from 2000 or 2008. Corporate earnings are still projected to grow at a healthy clip. Goldman Sachs forecasts S&P 500 earnings of $375 for 2026, $415 for 2027, and $460 for 2028.

When stocks fall while earnings rise, the only thing that's breaking is the multiple investors are willing to pay. The S&P 500's forward P/E has collapsed from roughly 23x a year ago to 16.5x today. That's a ~29% de-rating in about 13 months. We're also lower than we were during Liberation Day in April 2025.

In other words, the market isn't saying companies are making less money. It's saying it no longer trusts how fast AI profits will grow, and it wants a bigger margin of safety for the risk.

In a recent development, here's one of several rosy forecasts by Wall Street firms for year-end 2026 and 2027. I hope it comes true so that my wife and I can keep our FIRE membership card.

Industry observers note that at 6,910 and 16.5x, the implied forward earnings are about $418, which lines up neatly with Goldman's $415 estimate for 2027. So let's run the math using $418 in forward earnings.

In a recent development, the first takeaway is counterintuitive. At 16.5x, the S&P 500 is already cheaper than its 5-year and 10-year averages. If valuations simply mean revert to the past decade, the index has 16-20% of upside.

It has been revealed that the bear case indicates the last decade was the anomaly. Go back to 1990 on the Goldman chart and the aggregate index spent most of the 2003-2015 period between 13x and 17x. Revert to ~15x and the S&P falls another 7-8%. Revert to the 12.8x lows of the post-financial crisis era and we're looking at another ~23% drop.

Industry observers note that but the bigger risk isn't the multiple. It's the earnings. Here's what happens if AI spending gets throttled and forward earnings fall 10% to ~$376, essentially flat versus 2026.

The nightmare scenario requires both lower earnings and a lower multiple. That combination gets you to 5,600-5,700, or roughly 28% off the peak. Painful, but in line with a garden-variety bear market, not a 2000-style wipeout.

According to recent reports, my base case is that we're closer to the bottom than the top on valuation, but earnings revisions over the next two quarters will decide whether this is a correction or a bear market. Watch the earnings estimates, not the headlines.

When stock prices fall, CEOs get nervous and CFOs get busy. The easiest way to defend earnings per share is to cut the biggest expense line: people.

The layoffs were already happening before the selloff. Through October, tech companies unveiled 171,501 job cuts, 21% more than the same period a year earlier, and AI has been the top stated reason for cuts this year. Now add a 10%+ market correction and a Fed that's raising rates. I'm certain more mass layoffs are coming in Q1, after the bonuses are paid.

In a recent development, I lived through roughly 20 rounds of layoffs during my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse. The people who got cut first were rarely the least talented. They were the least liked, the least visible, and the most expensive relative to their output.

It has been revealed that so please be on your best behavior if you want to keep your job. Get in first, leave last, volunteer your time, and support your boss's charitable causes. It's corporate theater, but theater keeps the paychecks coming.

It has been revealed that if you don't want to deal with corporate BS anymore, start planning to negotiate a severance package now. The people who get laid off first tend to get the best severance packages. They also get a head start on the hundreds, if not thousands, of employees who will be looking for jobs later.

In a recent development, that's what I did in 2012. Instead of quitting, I negotiated my way out with a severance check that helped fund my first years of early retirement. I lay out the whole playbook in How To Engineer Your Layoff. Leaving a job you no longer like with a severance package feels incredible.

Most downturn advice assumes inflation is falling and the Fed is riding to the rescue with rate cuts. Not this time. When prices go up and asset values go down, you have to defend on four fronts at once.

Recent findings suggest that in a bull market, your portfolio can earn more than your salary. In this environment, your paycheck is the only asset that isn't getting marked down every day. Your job is now your most valuable asset, so treat it that way.

Be the person who uses AI to do the work of two people, not the person AI replaces. Build goodwill with your manager and colleagues before the layoff list gets made. And if you were thinking about quitting, don't. Stick around, collect your paychecks, and see if you can negotiate a severance when cuts inevitably hit your group.

According to recent reports, if you don't have a second income stream yet, start one now. It doesn't need to replace your salary. It just needs to cover your groceries, which feel like they cost a lot more than they used to. The key to financial freedom is generating enough passive income to cover your basic living expenses.

If you locked in a low fixed-rate mortgage, congratulations. Inflation is quietly shrinking your debt in real terms. This is not the time to aggressively pay it down and give up liquidity.

Sources indicate that with the Fed hiking, cash in a money market fund or Treasury bills finally pays you to wait. Earning over 5% risk-free in US Treasury bonds is a beautiful, beautiful thing.

Sources indicate that favor assets that can reprice with inflation. Rents and replacement costs tend to rise with prices, which is one reason I've always kept a large chunk of my net worth in real estate. Meanwhile, attack the variable expenses that are inflating fastest: gas, food, insurance, and subscriptions you forgot you had.

Personally, I'm eating less due to rising food costs, which is great for my dad bod challenge. I'm also just fixing my car instead of buying a fresh one. Finally, I've cut many superfluous items such as cable from our budget.

Instead of guessing the bottom, tie your purchases to the forward P/E. At ~$418 in forward earnings, 16x is about 6,690 on the S&P 500, 15x is about 6,270, and 14x is about 5,850. If we get down to these levels, buy a slug at each level and let the market come to you.

Before you buy anything, run a Financial SEER check. It's a way to quantify your risk tolerance, calculating potential loss in terms of time.

For example, if you have $500,000 in stocks and save $5,000 a month, another 20% drop costs you $100,000, or 20 months of work. If that makes you sick, you're already too aggressive, and buying more won't help you sleep.

Sources indicate that above all, avoid selling your best assets to fund a lifestyle that inflation made more expensive. That's how a temporary loss becomes a permanent one. Always stay disciplined when there's a chance we're heading into a zombie apocalypse.

If you're retired, this is a good time to lower your withdrawal rate and ride it out. As I wrote recently, FIRE in a bear market can actually be comforting. When Return On Effort falls, it's the perfect time to work less, not more.

If you have kids, a downturn is a gift. use corrections to help make your kids millionaires. During this selloff, I transferred $23,000 into each of my children's custodial accounts and bought stocks. The more the market fell on Friday, November 20, the more I transferred. And I will continue to transfer cash to their accounts and buy if the market goes lower.

According to recent reports, personally, I've accepted that I can't make money in the stock market right now. Every rally gets sold, and checking my portfolio feels hopeless. So I've stopped trying to fight it. I'm tired of the volatility.

According to recent reports, instead, I'm spending more time with my kids and fixing things around the house. For a couple of years, thick, heavy wallpaper had been peeling off in our downstairs hallway. It looked terrible, so I finally hired professionals to strip it, patch and sand, then prime and paint the walls. Then I spent an hour filling in imperfections and painting as well.

It looks great now. When the market won't reward your effort, put your money and energy into something you can actually see improve. This is why having an internal locus of control feels so good. You're not helpless.

And please keep living your life. The market doesn't care how miserable you are, so you might as well enjoy the holidays with your family.

It's easy to forget during a selloff, but downturns are temporary and time in the market is what builds wealth.

Recent findings suggest that bear markets transfer wealth from the impatient to the patient. They also reveal who was swimming naked with too much risk, too little cash, and too much confidence in their job security.

It has been revealed that you don't need to be a hero. You just need to survive with your job, your cash flow, and your sanity intact. Do that, and the next bull market will take care of the rest.

It has been revealed that readers, are you more worried about losing your job or losing more money in the markets? Where do you think the S&P 500 bottoms if earnings estimates start getting cut? Are you buying the dip in tranches, hoarding cash, or doing nothing at all? And for those who lived through 2000 and 2008 with a significant amount of capital, does this downturn feel different given how strong earnings still are?

In a recent development, invest In Real Estate To Diversify Away From Volatile Tech Stocks. AI is the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs compute, and compute needs physical data centers, power, and land. That's why I like real estate that benefits from the AI buildout without riding the daily swings of the Nasdaq. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

Recent findings suggest that A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

The main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

It has been revealed that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

Recent findings suggest that A recent study demonstrated that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

It has been revealed that there is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

There is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

Recent findings suggest that it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

According to recent reports, amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

Industry observers note that as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

Sources indicate that A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

It has been revealed that the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

According to recent reports, if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

In a recent development, chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

According to recent reports, the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

According to recent reports, later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Recent findings suggest that clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

It has been revealed that clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which revealed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

Sources indicate that clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

Industry observers note that if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how significant they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Industry observers note that clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

Sources indicate that in fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It has been revealed that it is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

Industry observers note that one history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

According to recent reports, as I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

Recent findings suggest that the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

Sources indicate that I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he shows to the world.”.
